extraction_text: Pulastya describes various sacred pilgrimage sites and their benefits to King Yudhishthira.
Pulastya describes the Dharma Tirtha, where bathing and following dharma purifies seven generations of one's family.
Pulastya describes the Kalapadana Tirtha, where one can gain the merit of performing an Agnihotra sacrifice and reach the world of sages.
Pulastya describes the Fragrant Forest (Gandhavana), where gods led by Brahma, sages, Siddhas, Charanas, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and Nagas reside, and entering it removes all sins.

Pulastya describes the Sarasvati River, the most excellent river that flows from a fig tree, where bathing in water flowing from an anthill and worshipping ancestors and gods grants the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
Pulastya describes the Svayambhu Tirtha, difficult to reach, where bathing grants the merit of a thousand Kapila cows and an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
Pulastya describes the pilgrimage to Gandha, Shatakumbha, and Panchayajna Tirthas, which brings respect in heaven.
Pulastya describes the Trishula Tirtha, where bathing and worshipping ancestors and gods grants the status of Ganapati after death.
Pulastya describes the difficult-to-reach goddess tirtha, Shakanvari, famous in the three worlds, where the goddess practiced vegetarianism for a thousand celestial years.
Sages, out of reverence for the goddess, went to Shakanvari, and she served them vegetables, earning her the name Shakanvari.
At Shakanvari, eating vegetables for three days yields the merit of eating vegetables for twelve years elsewhere, due to the goddess's grace.
Pulastya describes the Suvarnabindu Tirtha, where Vishnu pleased Rudra (Shiva) and sought boons.

attributes.significance: Confluence considered the yoni (womb) of the earth

extraction_text: Prayaga is described as having five sacred places: Pulayaga, Pulatistana, Kampala, Asvadara, and Bhagavati.

attributes.reward: Merit equivalent to major Vedic sacrifices
